subject: maths

moments.title: Pascal and Fermat correspond about gambling
moments.who: Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat (by letter)
moments.body:
A French nobleman, the Chevalier de Méré, asks Pascal about a gambling problem: how should the stakes be divided if a game of chance is interrupted before completion?

Pascal writes to Fermat. They develop the modern theory of probability through this correspondence. Their letters establish that probability can be calculated systematically, not just intuited.
moments.takeaway: Probability theory is born from a question about gambling.

moments.title: Bayes's theorem (posthumous)
moments.body:
Bayes, a Presbyterian minister and amateur mathematician, dies in 1761. His friend Richard Price finds an unpublished manuscript among his papers: 'An Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances'.

The paper contains what we now call Bayes's theorem: P(H | E) = P(E | H) * P(H) / P(E). It tells you how to update beliefs given new evidence. Price publishes it in 1763.

Bayes himself probably did not realise the full importance. Laplace develops the theorem fully decades later.
moments.takeaway: One of the most important results in probability is a posthumous paper its author thought of as a minor exercise.

moments.title: Laplace's Théorie Analytique
moments.body:
Laplace publishes the first comprehensive treatment of probability theory: 'Théorie Analytique des Probabilités'. He extends Bayes's work and applies it to astronomy, demography, jurisprudence.

Laplace's view: probability is degree of belief, updateable by evidence. This Bayesian view dominates 19th-century probability.
moments.takeaway: Probability becomes a tool for inference about the world, not just gambling odds.

moments.title: Fisher and the frequentist turn
moments.who: R. A. Fisher, Rothamsted Experimental Station
moments.body:
Ronald Fisher reframes statistics around frequencies and hypothesis testing. His 'Statistical Methods for Research Workers' (1925) introduces p-values, ANOVA, design of experiments. He is hostile to Bayesian methods, partly because they require specifying a prior.

For most of the 20th century, frequentist methods dominate. Bayesian probability is marginalised — except in a few corners (Jeffreys, Jaynes, de Finetti).
moments.takeaway: Probability splits into rival schools: frequentist (probability = long-run frequency) vs Bayesian (probability = degree of belief).

moments.title: Bayesian revival
moments.who: Multiple — statistical computing, machine learning communities
moments.body:
Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods (MCMC) make Bayesian computation feasible. Bayesian methods become dominant in machine learning, medical diagnosis, search-engine ranking, navigation.

The Bayesian/frequentist 'war' is now mostly seen as a false dichotomy — practitioners use whichever framework fits the problem.
moments.takeaway: Bayesian probability comes back, driven by computational tractability and practical success.

now.title: Probability today
now.body:
Probability theory is rigorously based on measure theory (Kolmogorov, 1933). Modern statistical methods combine frequentist and Bayesian elements. Probabilistic programming languages let researchers specify complex models and let the computer handle inference.

Applications: weather forecasting, financial modelling, genome-wide association studies, machine learning, autonomous vehicles, drug trials, search engines.
now.open_questions: What is the right interpretation of probability for one-shot events? Can the foundations of probability be made more philosophically secure? Why are some natural distributions (Gaussian, Poisson, power laws) so ubiquitous? How should we communicate probabilistic results to non-statisticians?

reflection: Bayes's paper was published two years after his death by a friend who thought it was important. Without Price's intervention, Bayes's theorem might have been credited to Laplace alone. How much of mathematical history depends on chance recoveries of work the author didn't think was particularly important?
